notes.meaning: Moses was amazed when he saw a bush burning with fire but not burning up. As he walked closer to investigate the strange sight, God spoke directly to him out of the flames. God used this wonder to get Moses' full attention before giving him His holy message.

God identified Himself as the same God who made promises to Moses' ancestors long ago. Hearing the voice of the Almighty made Moses shake with fear, so he did not dare to look. Because God is still the God of these faithful men even after their earthly deaths, it shows they are still alive with Him.

Taking off sandals was an ancient sign of deep reverence and respect before God. The ground became holy simply because the presence of the living God was there, not because the dirt itself was special. Stephen emphasized this to remind the council that God's presence was never confined to their temple in Jerusalem.

God told Moses that He had witnessed every pain and heard every cry of His suffering people in Egypt. The Lord declared that He had come to rescue them, and He appointed Moses to carry out this mission. Even though Moses had run away forty years earlier, God was now sending him back with divine authority.

Stephen reminded his hearers that the Israelites had originally rejected Moses when he tried to step in as their judge. Yet God chose that very same rejected man to be their leader and deliverer. In the same way, the Jewish leaders had recently rejected Jesus, whom God appointed as the true Savior.

Moses proved his divine calling by doing mighty miracles in Egypt, parting the Red Sea, and guiding the people through the desert for forty years. These miracles were clear signs that God was actively working through him. Stephen honored Moses' great leadership, showing that the charges against Stephen were completely false.

Moses had foretold that God would one day send another prophet from among their own people who would be like him. Stephen pointed out that this promised prophet was Jesus Christ. By rejecting Jesus, the Jewish leaders were actually refusing to obey Moses, who had told them to listen to Him.

Moses served as a mediator, a go-between who stood between God's angel on Mount Sinai and the gathering of Israel in the desert. There he received God's laws, which are described as living words because they carry active, life-giving power. Stephen honored this law deeply, proving he was not guilty of speaking against it.

Despite all God's wonders, the people rebelled against Moses and pushed his leadership aside. In their hearts, they longed for the false gods and comforts of Egypt rather than trusting God in the wilderness. Stephen used this history to show that the nation had an old habit of disobeying God's chosen servants.

While Moses was up on the mountain receiving God's laws, the people grew impatient and demanded visible idols to lead them. They spoke disrespectfully of Moses and acted as if they could easily replace both him and God. Their demand exposed how quickly human hearts can turn to man-made religion when their faith is tested.

The Israelites crafted a golden idol in the shape of a calf, copying the animal worship they had seen in Egypt. They offered sacrifices to this statue and celebrated around a god they had manufactured with their own hands. Stephen reminded his listeners that making an idol out of human work is pure rebellion against God.

Because Israel abandoned God, He stepped back and allowed them to slide into worse idolatry, worshipping the sun, moon, and stars. Stephen quoted the prophet Amos to show that even during the forty years in the desert, their sacrifices were insincere and divided. God rejects outward rituals when people's hearts are secretly devoted to idols.

Israel carried portable shrines and star-symbols for false gods like Molech and Rephan instead of staying loyal to the Lord. Because they chose false gods, God announced that He would send them far away into exile as prisoners. Stephen cited Babylon to remind them how idolatry had led to the ruin of their nation in the past.

Stephen began answering the charge of speaking against the temple by recalling the original tent of worship, the tabernacle. Moses built it strictly according to the heavenly blueprint God revealed on Mount Sinai. It was called the tent of testimony because it held the stone tablets of the law, which proved God's covenant with His people.

The next generation inherited this holy tent and carried it into the promised land under Joshua's leadership. God cleared out the pagan nations before them, and the movable tabernacle remained Israel's place of worship for centuries until King David's reign. This proved that God had accepted worship long before any permanent temple was ever built.

David enjoyed God's special favor and deeply desired to build a permanent house for Him. Even though David's wish was noble, God did not permit him to build it because he had been a man of war. God's presence had never depended on a building made of stone.

It was David's son Solomon who finally constructed the temple in Jerusalem. While building the temple honored God, it was a late arrival in Israel's history. The nation had flourished under God's guidance for hundreds of years before this building ever existed.

Solomon himself admitted that no earthly building could ever contain the infinite God. Stephen rebuked the religious leaders for treating the temple like an idol, as if God were locked inside walls made by humans. True worship is spiritual and cannot be restricted to any single building.

Quoting the prophet Isaiah, Stephen pointed out that God rules the entire universe as His throne and footstool. Since God created everything that exists, no person can construct a home that adds anything to His glory. Therefore, God's work could never be destroyed just because an earthly temple might fall.

Stephen boldly challenged his listeners, comparing them to stubborn oxen that refuse to bow to a yoke. Although they were physically circumcised, their hearts were closed to God and their ears refused to listen to His truth. Just as their ancestors opposed God's messengers in the past, these leaders were actively fighting against the Holy Spirit.

differ.view: Methodists believe people have genuine freedom to resist and reject the Holy Spirit's convicting work.
Reformed Christians believe that while all people naturally resist the Spirit, God's grace overcomes this resistance in the elect.

notes.meaning: Stephen asked the council to name a single prophet their ancestors had not mistreated. The ancient leaders had murdered the messengers who foretold the coming Messiah, the Righteous One. The present council had now outdone their ancestors by betraying and murdering that Messiah Himself.

The Jewish leaders took great pride in possessing the law of Moses, which had been delivered with the glorious attendance of angels. Yet despite this holy privilege, Stephen charged that they constantly broke the very law they claimed to protect. Their outward pride could not hide their inward disobedience.

Stephen's words cut deep into the consciences of the council members, but instead of repenting, they exploded with furious anger. They ground their teeth at him like savage beasts ready to tear their prey. Their blind rage revealed how completely their hearts rejected God's truth.

Completely controlled and comforted by the Holy Spirit, Stephen turned his eyes away from his angry accusers and looked straight into heaven. God granted him a vision of divine splendor, showing Jesus standing in the place of highest honor next to the Father. While Scripture usually describes Jesus as sitting in heaven, here He stands as if rising to welcome, honor, and defend His brave servant.

Stephen openly told the hostile court what he was seeing. By calling Jesus the Son of Man, he echoed the exact words Jesus had used when on trial before this very council. This confirmed that the crucified Jesus was alive, exalted, and ruling in heaven.

The leaders clamped their hands over their ears to avoid hearing what they considered terrible blasphemy. They shouted loudly to drown out his voice and charged at him as an uncontrolled mob. Their extreme anger drove them past any normal legal procedures.

The mob hauled Stephen outside the city walls so they would not defile the city by shedding blood there. The witnesses, who were legally required to throw the first stones, took off their outer robes to throw more easily and left them in the care of a young leader named Saul. This is the Bible's first mention of Saul, who would later become the apostle Paul.

Even while heavy stones were crushing his body, Stephen focused entirely on prayer. He addressed Jesus directly as Lord and asked Him to welcome his departing soul into heaven. Praying directly to Jesus in this way was a clear act of worship that recognized Jesus as truly God.

Dropping to his knees, Stephen shouted a final prayer asking the Lord to forgive the very men who were killing him, just as Jesus had done on the cross. After uttering these loving words, he died so peacefully that the Bible describes it simply as falling asleep. His body rested from its earthly pain while his spirit went directly to be with Christ.
